body:
MEASURED 2026-08-29 across one evening of concurrent work.

WHAT IT COSTS. `findings/INDEX.md` is regenerated by `scripts/findings.py index` and its header line
carries running totals ("249 open, 37 closed"). EVERY findings-touching PR rewrites that line, so any
two such PRs conflict pairwise no matter how unrelated their findings are. Observed in one evening:

  * three submit cycles lost to `merge-blocked (CONFLICTING)` / `head-moved` / `DIRTY` across four of
    my own PRs, each needing rebase + regenerate + force-push + gate rebind;
  * #1956 reported BEHIND three consecutive times before it could land, which is what prompted a
    fleet-wide 25-minute merge freeze;
  * a delegate added a finding JSON WITHOUT regenerating the index, and nothing caught it.

NOTHING READS IT. Verified by grep across *.py, *.sh, *.yml, *.ts: the only programmatic reference is
`scripts/findings.py`, which WRITES it (`INDEX = ROOT / "findings" / "INDEX.md"`, and the `index`
subcommand). `tests/unit/test_findings_ledger.py` monkeypatches `INDEX` to a tmp_path, so no test
reads the real file. Its only consumers are three markdown documents that link to it and a human
browsing the repo on GitHub. So the conflicts buy nothing: the artifact is a rendering of
`findings/items/*.json`, which is the actual source of truth and which almost never conflicts,
because separate findings are separate files.

OPTIONS, in the order I would consider them.

  (a) Keep it tracked, but stop carrying it on feature branches: PRs change only
      `findings/items/*.json`, and a small job regenerates INDEX.md on `main` after merge. Branches
      then have nothing to conflict over, the GitHub-browsable index stays current, and the
      "delegate forgot to regenerate" failure mode disappears because regeneration is no longer a
      human step. This is the standard treatment for a generated artifact and is my recommendation.

  (b) Keep the current workflow but remove the running-totals line from the header, and keep rows
      grouped so that unrelated findings land in different sections. Most conflicts collapse to that
      single line; this is a cheap partial fix if (a) is unwanted.

  (c) Untrack it entirely and generate on demand. Cheapest to implement, but it removes the
      browsable index, which is the file's whole purpose. Not recommended.

⚠️ THIS IS A SHARED-WORKFLOW CHANGE, NOT A LOCAL ONE. Roughly ten sessions open PRs against this repo
concurrently, and (a) changes what every one of them must do. It should be agreed through the
dispatcher rather than landed unilaterally by whichever session happens to file this. Raised there
alongside this entry.

Until it is decided, the working rule stands and is recorded in project memory: regenerate the index
with the script, never hand-resolve a conflict inside it, land findings-touching PRs sequentially,
and eyeball the result before pushing.

---

## 2026-08-29 — it is worse than conflicts: the file can merge CLEANLY into a corrupt state

Everything above treats the cost as *conflicts* — annoying, but they stop you, so you fix them.
Observed tonight while merging `origin/main` into `findings/bulk-membership`: the merge reported
success, no conflict, and produced this:

```
251 open, 37 closed.
250 open, 40 closed.
```

**Two count lines.** Both sides had edited the single summary line, at different offsets relative
to their surrounding table rows, so git's line-based merge kept *both* rather than conflicting.
The result is a generated file that states two different totals, committed by a merge that
looked clean.

This inverts the finding's severity. A conflict is a stop sign — noisy, but self-announcing. This
is a silent semantic corruption in a file nobody reads closely *because it is generated*, and the
only reason it was caught is that I happened to re-run `scripts/findings.py index` and diff the
result, which is not a step anyone is required to take:

```
cp findings/INDEX.md /tmp/i1.md
python3 scripts/findings.py index
diff /tmp/i1.md findings/INDEX.md     # <- the only thing that surfaced it
```

Nothing in CI checks that `INDEX.md` matches `findings/items/*.json`. So a corrupt index can
merge to main and stay there until someone regenerates for an unrelated reason.

**This strengthens recommendation (a)** — stop carrying the generated file on branches and
regenerate it post-merge on main — and it adds a second, independently valuable guard that is
worth having even if (a) never ships: **a CI check that regenerates the index and fails if the
committed copy differs.** That check is three lines, catches this class outright, and would also
have caught the several occasions this cycle where a delegate edited `findings/items/` and forgot
to regenerate.

The proposal to block PRs that touch both `findings/items/` and `INDEX.md` does NOT cover this
case, and would not have caught it: here neither side did anything wrong. Each branch legitimately
added a finding and legitimately regenerated. The corruption is created by the *merge*, which no
per-PR rule can see.
title: findings/INDEX.md is a generated file carried on every branch, making it the repo's largest merge-conflict surface for no functional benefit
